doc.title: Reggie Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

title: Studio time and recording the Knepper album
summary: Two days in a Brooklyn studio, semi-live setup, and choosing takes from fifteen or sixteen songs.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Terrific. When you do a record date like that how much time do you get in the studio?

It depends on your funding. It depends on your funding. So I did two days. Everything for that was preparation and getting the charts in order, rehearsing, and then going into the studio, kind of a pricey studio, you know, in Brooklyn, so we were two days in the studio. And that was enough.
Does it take a while to get used to the fact that there is some separation in the studio, the drummer may be behind a glass house or whatever.

It does. In that studio, although we could have been completely separated, we purposely didn’t do that. So like the bass player was in a booth but the door was open and he was kind of out. Piano was out in the open, horns were facing piano and drums. Maybe the drums had a little bit of soundproof. But we were all looking at each other right here. You know. So it was somewhat live.
Is everybody involved, all the players, are they all involved in the choosing of the best take?

Yes. Well people can weigh in. But when the session is over you still have two or three takes of each tune that, you know, the buck stops with whoever is producing the record. So we had to eventually —
Yeah. So we had a lot of material to go through, and there was a lot we didn’t use you know. Because we probably recorded fifteen, sixteen songs, several takes.
And we wanted to go with — for a long list of reasons you pick what you pick you know?
